source.title: An Effective and Efficient Training Algorithm for Multi-layer Feedforward Neural Networks
source.authors: Zebin Yang; Hengtao Zhang; A. Sudjianto; Aijun Zhang

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper. Its title is “An Effective and Efficient Initialization Scheme for Training Multi-layer Feedforward Neural Networks,” which differs from the catalog TITLE; no other document problem is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares initialization methods and reports their training-loss trajectories in deep tanh networks, bearing on initialization’s effect on training speed. It does not test the stated CIFAR classification-error claims or the specific 10,000-layer convolutional result.
record.gate_note: Figures 2–3 report training-loss trajectories averaged over datasets and 10 repetitions; the text says SteinGLM converges much faster and the three benchmarks can get stuck in less optimal solutions. Test-set RMSE and AUC tables do not measure the training-error outcomes named in V1. Cited findings from other work are not extracted as this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares training-loss trajectories under different initializations in 10–40-layer plain tanh networks, testing V4's initialization-dependent training-speed component. It does not test V3's depth degradation or shortcut comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that SteinGLM improves training speed and prediction accuracy against the tested benchmarks in feedforward networks. Their MNIST CNN demonstration converges faster but shows no significant validation or test-performance difference. They acknowledge normal-input assumptions and restriction to sigmoid and tanh activations.
record.recipe_differences: SteinGLM uses response-informed second-order Stein estimates for hidden-layer weights and GLM for the output layer, rather than the cited random or orthogonal initializations. The experiments use tanh feedforward networks and a small CNN demonstration.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper varies initialization method, network depth, and task. Its text reports faster SteinGLM convergence across the regression and binary-classification trajectory summaries; it does not give separate numerical training-loss values by dataset or depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Tables 2–5 compare test RMSE and AUC, including GLM ablations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Response-informed initialization can improve held-out prediction performance in the tested tabular networks.

record.problems: Training-loss trajectories are averaged across datasets and 10 repetitions, and the text gives no exact trajectory values or uncertainty for them. The text groups benchmark methods when describing local stalls, without identifying which individual methods or settings account for the result. Experiments are on tabular datasets and a small MNIST demonstration, not CIFAR benchmarks.
record.rows_left_out: Test-set RMSE and AUC results in Tables 2–5 were not extracted as rows because they do not measure training speed or the training-error effects named by the tested versions. The paper reports CNN training-loss curves in Figure 5 and says SteinGLM converges faster, but does not report the depth, initialization-specific numeric losses, or uncertainty for each digit-pair condition; that demonstration is outside the tested V3/V4 feedforward tanh conditions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization.
ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious-minimum frequencies, and benefits of extra student neurons.
Higher training error with increasing depth in plain batch-normalized CNNs, longer-training controls, identity-shortcut comparisons, very deep plain tanh training, and Fixup.

Direct measurements of vanishing or exploding signals and gradients; activation-matching as the cause of improvement; maximum trainable depth; matched-variance orthogonal-versus-Gaussian comparisons; and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Stability thresholds, curvature or sharpness trajectories, catapult recovery, and divergence.
Batch-normalization comparisons, higher-learning-rate tolerance, and normalization-free Fixup training.

missing.what: The ablation discussion explicitly reports training stalls when GLM output initialization is combined with He Normal or Glorot Normal hidden-layer initialization. Add condition-specific qualitative rows; the test-metric tables alone cannot quantify these stalls.
missing.locator: Section 3.3, paragraph beginning with the contribution of GLM initialization, continuing after Table 2

record.verdict_notes: Do not retain the V3 support verdict or the V4 limits_scope verdict based solely on benchmark stalls: V4 does not promise that every named initializer succeeds with tanh. SteinGLM uses responses during initialization and fits the output layer before subsequent training, so these comparisons concern the full initialization procedures. Figures are represented only by captions in the supplied text; individual curve values cannot be checked. Figure 5 is already declared in rows_left_out, so it is not an undeclared missing result. Contrary to that declaration's rationale, Section 3.4 specifies nine convolutional layers and a fully connected hidden layer; its reported faster convergence also bears on V4's training-speed component.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, corrupted or random labels, and the effects of model size, early stopping, and regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima rates, and student width relative to teacher width.

The plain batch-normalized versus residual comparison on ImageNet/CIFAR-10, and Fixup’s residual-network results without normalization. The study uses 10–40-layer tanh feedforward networks and does not report a shortcut comparison.

The specific Gaussian-versus-orthogonal comparisons in very deep tanh networks and orthogonal convolutional networks at 10,000 layers. The study compares SteinGLM with Glorot Normal, He Normal, and Orthogonal initialization in 10–40-layer tanh feedforward networks.
Learning-rate stability limits, loss rises, curvature or sharpness, and divergence.
Batch normalization’s effect on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup results for residual networks without normalization.
